title: Stagflation, Regime Change, and the Clues We Missed - Systematic Investor 347

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/Stagflation, Regime Change, and the Clues We Missed - Systematic Investor 347.docx

speakers: Jim Kasang (Chicago macro/options-flow strategist, caption spelling)
summary: Jim argues populism and tariffs create a slow stagflation (hot inflation, margin squeeze) like 1969-70, with refinancing cliffs draining liquidity and raising discount rates, so assets fall together. He calls for diversification beyond long assets, oil mean reversion, and options-expiry flow cycles for the S&P outlook, with fourth-turning narrative.

coverage.note: intro/sponsor; Buffett retirement; liquidity from 5-year refinancing
Buffett and inflation, fourth turning, Taiwan dollar, politics
CTA performance data; populism, redistribution and inflation
stagflation shape, 1969-70 analog, top-10% spending, tariffs and jobs
tariff jobs, inflation basket (software), debt issuance and incentives
Fed in a box, supply-side plan fails
Nixon analogy, US CDS and tail risk, monetization
rate lag and refinancing cliff, liquidity draw
60/40 danger, discount rates, inflation hedges, oil, dollar
dollar and inflation, oil as policy lever, reflexive oil
Saudi supply, oil buy view, Kofenas episode intro

technical levels, opex flows, seasonality, administration support

completeness_estimate: 0.75 - first reader (48 claims) caught the core thesis (populism to stagflation, refinancing cliff, discount-rate shock, oil mean reversion, opex flows); 17 additions are index data points, refinancing-wall shape and term-choice reasoning, OPEC squeeze mechanism, opex seasonality reason and caveats; no misstatements found.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: we're reaching the 5-year anniversary of the refinancing of of debt
claims.claim: Debt, venture and equity financing raised at 2020 lows (about five-year terms) comes due around 2025, pulling liquidity out of the system and stressing even cash-poor elite endowments.
claims.testable: partly - maturity walls are observable, impact timing is not

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: Insurance the one thing he started with by definition is a negative working capital business that excels during times of inflation.
claims.claim: Negative-working-capital businesses such as insurance gain in inflation as margins rise and offset multiple contraction, which is why Buffett outperformed in the 1970s inflation.
claims.direction: long insurance / negative working capital firms in inflation
claims.testable: yes - sort stocks by working capital in inflation regimes

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: much like the fourth turning does right because of these generational things
claims.claim: Generational cycles (the fourth turning, 40-50 years) repeat conditions such as inflation and populism, so history from the 1960s-70s is a template.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the short-term traders index doing obviously better in this environment
claims.claim: In early 2025 SG trend was down about 10% YTD and the CTA index 7.5%, while the short-term traders index was only about -1%, so shorter horizons held up.
claims.indicator: SG Trend, SG CTA, SG Short-Term Traders index

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: Moving it to the bottom 40% then creates inflation because the the velocity of that money
claims.claim: Populist transfers from the top 10% to the bottom 40% raise velocity because lower-income households spend everything, while the top puts money into assets, so inflation rises.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: particularly under a protectionist type scenario where it becomes things become more inefficient are less profits for corporations
claims.claim: Protectionism with populism gives more jobs but lower pay, higher inflation and lower corporate margins, so profits fall.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: If you look at 1969 1970 as our most recent example of something like this, you know, you saw a very very shallow kind of one and a half two-year recession
claims.claim: The 1969-70 analog is a shallow 1.5-year recession with poor earnings and equities rather than a deep V recession.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: it wasn't a time when the 10-year bond kind of came down and helped with poor equity performance because inflation was sticky
claims.claim: In stagflation the long bond does not rally to offset equity declines because inflation is sticky, so bonds fail as a hedge.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: the top 10% is now 50% of retail spending in the United States
claims.claim: Because the top 10% account for half of spending, a wealth-effect hit would cut consumption, giving an earnings recession with margin compression while jobs stay stable.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: I'm here to tell you I think it's actually uh more inflation
claims.claim: Consensus expects a deep recession with disinflation; the speaker expects a mild, slow recession with hot inflation, i.e. stagflation of the high-inflation kind.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: if there's a reason they're staying pat is because they know one thing and they're not sure about the other
claims.claim: The Fed holds because inflation effects from tariffs are certain while the growth effect is uncertain.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: those supply chains will have to be repopulated somebody has to take those jobs that is massive demand for jobs
claims.claim: Reshoring after tariffs raises prices and creates a rush of local job demand, so it is inflationary before it hits margins; timing of recession vs GDP is unclear.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: He's right on our basket of like uh you know, stocks that will outperform in in periods of structural inflation
claims.claim: Basket for structural inflation: insurance, value/DCF names, software and telecom, which raise revenue and margins; growth software relying on venture money suffers.
claims.testable: yes - sector returns in inflation regimes

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: people respond to incentives
claims.claim: Treasury issuance (short-dated) and Fed pressure follow political incentives under both parties, so short-termism in debt policy is structural.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: In terms of the Federal Reserve, they're in a box.
claims.claim: The Fed is stuck between inflation and growth, with a shrinking set of choices, as Burns was in the 1970s, and populist politics add to it.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: and tax cuts to the rich and a hope that if they push the market down enough that the Fed would react, right, and get the 10-year down
claims.claim: The administration's early supply-side plan assumed a market drop would make the Fed cut and lower the 10-year; it failed in a month, ending the plan.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: populism is what's trying to fix that inequality
claims.claim: Inequality drives populism, so politics will keep moving toward spending on the bottom and away from supply-side policy.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: Congress is now trying to pass no taxes on any tips. That is a huge deal.
claims.claim: Policy shifted to populist fiscal measures (no tax on tips, defense +$150bn a year) with spending cuts reversed.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: Didn't last long before it got to price controls and Watergate.
claims.claim: As in the Nixon era, a short supply-side try gave way to more populist and interventionist policy.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: It's the one thing that everybody's short is the tail.
claims.claim: Tiny-probability tail risks (US default) can move CDS and bond markets sharply because the tail is unhedgeable; vol rises more in the tail than at the money (skew).

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: Monetize, right? So, so um but uh and by the way, I do think that's going to happen.
claims.claim: Faced with unsustainable debt the US would monetize rather than default.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: If you have a significant decline to historically low interest rates like zero, guess what? There is a massive amount of refinancing and capital that gets stored away for the winter, right?
claims.claim: The lag between rate rises and market damage lengthens after rates hit zero because borrowers locked in five-year financing; the later hit is bigger (reason for Shiller's smoothed 10-year CAPE).

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: that's going to be importantly a draw in liquidity from somewhere else
claims.claim: When many borrowers (VC, sovereign debt) refinance at the same time at lower valuations, it draws liquidity from other assets, pushing prices down.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: the idea that we need to diversify away from just owning assets is not part of the vernacular
claims.claim: 60/40 and private alternatives are all long assets exposed to the same discount-rate and liquidity risk; real diversification needs trend following or non-correlated strategies.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: If an if if the tenure goes up the earnings yield of what you need to make in any asset any asset right that has to go up which means price has to go down.
claims.claim: A higher 10-year yield raises the required return on every asset so prices fall; the discount-rate shock matters more than earnings.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: equities despite people thinking they're a hedge to inflation are not and have not historically been
claims.claim: Equities are not an inflation hedge because multiples fall as inflation rises, even if assets hold value.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: It is a good inflationary hedge.
claims.claim: Oil keeps value relative to inflation (margins don't compress) but in a liquidity drain or mild recession it still falls, though less than other assets.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: We're moving buyers right when the selling is coming on the market.
claims.claim: Foreign buyers are being alienated while supply of assets for sale rises, causing dollar weakness and a lower ceiling for US equities.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: Dollar weakness has a reflexive effect of causing more inflation
claims.claim: A weaker dollar raises import prices, so dollar weakness feeds inflation on top of tariffs.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: Incentives always rule the day. Trump has a problem. He has an inflationary problem.
claims.claim: The administration's main inflation lever is oil, via US production and Saudi supply, so oil prices are pushed lower; early-2025 oil shorts were profitable.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: one of the easiest m ways to make money in the long run is when oil gets really cheap to buy it and when oil gets really expensive to sell it
claims.claim: Oil is highly reflexive, with cheap prices cutting supply and expensive prices adding supply, so mean reversion pays but slowly (not a one-year trade).
claims.direction: buy when cheap, sell when expensive

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: Trump wants lower oil. They're willing to do it. Doesn't cost them anything.
claims.claim: Saudi/OPEC supply increases serve the long game and favour the US administration, so supply can be set outside normal supply-demand forces.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: there's going to be a generational buy opportunity in oil okay and oil names
claims.claim: In roughly 9-15 months oil will offer a generational buying opportunity after the asset-deflation period.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: all the the entities that uh that don't make money below 40
claims.claim: Below about $40 many producers lose money, which forces supply cuts reflexively and Saudi budgets strain.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: this idea of crisis um that you and I have talked about and a need for crisis in order to kind of resolve these problems
claims.claim: Structural problems resolve only through a crisis (the fourth turning), after which a new regime begins; outcome depends on unity, per Campbell's hero's journey.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: the one thing at this time of coming crisis that is critical is unity or the ability to unify.
claims.claim: Unity decides whether the West meets the coming crisis; disunity (including from outside actors) is a risk factor.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: confidence, your time horizon gets short.
claims.claim: Low confidence shortens time horizons (as in short-dated Treasury issuance), per Peter Atwater.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: maybe the true structural threat is already largely um you know undisussed
claims.claim: As in 2007, crowds debate recession while a structural flaw (now Treasury market dysfunction) may be the real risk, so the real danger may be unspoken.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: So hard to predict the actual tail, but the distribution is is easier, right?
claims.claim: With fat tails everywhere and many policy variables now dynamic, one cannot predict the tail event but can plan for a wide leptokurtic distribution.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: we now have a catalyst to increased uncertainty in the world of a high potential energy situation
claims.claim: Many things assumed static (tariffs, alliances) are now dynamic and interact, so uncertainty is rising where stored pressure is high (sumo market).

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Diversification is not about making more money. It's about actually building something that's resilient.
claims.claim: Diversification buys resilience, not return, and has not paid off while seven stocks or one index dominated; passive may revert to active.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: that ceiling has come down and our most recent kind of uh predictions were somewhere between 5700 and 6,000 likely
claims.claim: After the Feb-Mar drop and a rally, S&P 500 upside was capped around 5700-6000 as tariffs and politics worsened.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: when there's a confluence of different things and uh that usually matters a lot
claims.claim: Resistance forms where several technical levels line up (such as the 200-day average); multiple confluent levels matter more than one.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: particularly on tops it's more of a process it always is right
claims.claim: Market tops form through a process, not a V reversal, so after a drop and rally the high may still be in a topping range.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: CO started the day after Feb opex. It ended the day after March opex.
claims.claim: Quarterly options expiration cycles drive flows: Covid and the 2025 decline started right after Feb opex and ended at March opex; June is usually less bad than March.
claims.direction: S&P weak from Feb opex to March opex

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: This is why sell in May, by the way, happens.
claims.claim: Calendar adages such as sell in May reflect repeating structural flow cycles (options expiry, year-end ramp).

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: is trying to juice the market clearly and trying to push a deal through and show some positive momentum to support this market
claims.claim: The administration pushes deal announcements to support the market, and a smaller-than-expected deal would pull risk forward.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: What's the most important thing for this market right now? The 10-year inflation.
claims.claim: The 10-year yield and inflation data (CPI) are the central market drivers, and when option-cycle flows and key levels meet an event, the risk is concentrated.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: And the S&P 500 up 1.13% in May so far, down only 3.85% so far this year.
claims.claim: By 8 May 2025, after the April tariff shock, the S&P 500 was only -3.85% YTD, MSCI World about flat and the aggregate bond index +2.5%, while trend followers were far worse (BTOP50 -4.22%, SG CTA -7.5%, SG Trend about -10%), so the V-shaped reversal whipsawed trend followers more than it hurt a passive stock-bond mix.
claims.indicator: BTOP50, SG CTA, SG Trend, S&P 500, MSCI World and bond aggregate YTD returns
claims.direction: trend followers lag in sharp reversals
claims.testable: yes - index returns over the same window

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: my own trend barometer stands at 50 has been around
claims.claim: Niels's own trend barometer sat at 50 (neutral to slightly positive) for weeks, signalling weak trend strength that matches the poor trend-follower performance despite a small recovery.
claims.direction: weak trend strength means less trend-following upside
claims.testable: partly - barometer is a proprietary measure

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Some of the same themes are continuing gold doing well. You know, even some of the agricultural markets like live cattle um doing well, equities still being supported.
claims.claim: In early May 2025 the trends that kept paying were gold and live cattle, with equities still supported and the dollar regaining part of April's loss, while the month was quiet after a wild April.
claims.indicator: gold, live cattle, equities, dollar trends
claims.direction: long gold and live cattle trends

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: you can think about some jobs being replaced by robots. Obviously, that's not necessarily inflationary
claims.claim: Niels adds that how reshored jobs are filled changes the inflation effect: automation would not be inflationary, while an immigration crackdown removes the low-paid labour that would otherwise fill them, adding wage pressure.
claims.testable: no - qualitative caveat to the reshoring-inflation argument

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: Vulker was not a hero. You know he just right he had the ability to do a big thing at a big
claims.claim: Fed chairs squeezed between inflation and growth (Burns, Powell) get cast as fools, while Volcker looked heroic mainly because he had room to act decisively at the right time; the current Fed's set of choices keeps shrinking.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: politically in the first 100 days is the worst approval rating in since 1940
claims.claim: The supply-side plan failed politically as well as on rates: the first 100 days saw the worst approval rating since 1940, which pushed the administration back toward its populist base.
claims.testable: partly - approval data exist, link to policy is argued

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: they've abandoned the supply side old school Republican corporate interest supply side economic model
claims.claim: The administration was always an unstable equilibrium between supply-side business interests and populist protectionists; with the supply-side faction out and the populists in charge, investors should not expect a business-friendly policy mix.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: Trump knows if he's going to survive in the midterms in a year and a half, he's got to get back on that
claims.claim: The midterm incentive forces a pivot back to populist, bottom-income-friendly policy, so the political drift toward spending and away from supply-side policy is likely to persist.
claims.direction: more spending on the bottom, fewer cuts

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: nobody's going to take money when it's super cheap for one year, right? But but also, you know, there's a cost to taking money for 10 years in some situations.
claims.claim: When money is cheap borrowers lock in around five years, not one (too short) and not ten (too costly), so financing raised at the 2020 low clusters its refinancing in a narrow window around 2025.
claims.indicator: debt and equity maturity profile of 2020-21 financing
claims.direction: refinancing demand concentrated in one period
claims.conditions: financing raised near the rate low
claims.testable: yes - maturity data by issuance year

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: they got to raise money guess where valuations are 75% of or 25% of where they were or 30% or 40% or whatever they are
claims.claim: Example: a venture-backed firm that raised in the 2020-21 boom, expecting ten years of cash that lasted five, must raise again at valuations far below the peak (caption garbled, roughly a quarter to 40% of earlier levels), so refinancing absorbs liquidity from other assets.
claims.testable: partly - anecdotal, venture data could test it

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: there's actually a period where it kind of slows down a bit and then kicks us again and and by then if interest rates are even higher then we have an even bigger problem
claims.claim: The refinancing overhang rises, levels off and slows, then re-accelerates; if rates are higher when it kicks in again the problem is larger, so the liquidity drain is not a one-off event.
claims.indicator: refinancing wall by year versus interest-rate level
claims.conditions: rates higher at the time of the second wave
claims.testable: yes - maturity wall data and rates

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: they didn't counter the US for some time, right? Because they thought too much supply was coming on the market from the US
claims.claim: OPEC/Saudi supply is a tool: after tolerating US supply growth for a time, they add supply to squeeze high-cost producers when they judge there is too much, and remove it otherwise, and can repeat this again and again.
claims.indicator: OPEC supply decisions versus US output
claims.direction: oil prices set by OPEC supply moves rather than demand
claims.testable: partly - OPEC decisions versus price moves are testable

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: it's fine to put tariffs against the counterparty but if you're doing it against your allies this is the west
claims.claim: Jim sees tariffs on allies, with a stated closeness to Russia, as disunifying the West, which he treats as a risk factor for the coming crisis (and a sign that the policy maker may be a 'useful fool').
claims.indicator: tariffs on allies; Western alliance cohesion

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: collapse of belief in America's ability and willingness to stand behind it its own debt
claims.claim: Niels flags a loss of confidence in the US ability and willingness to honour its debt as the scenario to watch, linking to Atwater's confidence work and the Treasury market dysfunction as a possible unspoken structural threat.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: We said it would be steep initially before all the tariff stuff we said that might get back to 6,000 or new highs
claims.claim: Conditional forecast track record: after the Feb-March drop (about 15%, later 21%) he called a steep rally toward 6,000 or new highs, then lowered the ceiling after the tariff news and political changes; the S&P reached about 5,720 that week.
claims.conditions: tariff and political news change the ceiling

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: I'm not the only one that looks at them and that's important.
claims.claim: Technical levels matter because many participants watch the same levels (200-day average and others), which makes the resistance partly self-fulfilling.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: we usually get a big ramp into end of the year January, which then if we can hang on through Feb, then kind of creates potential energy for March.
claims.claim: Mechanism for the options-cycle pattern: the year-end and January ramp stores potential energy that tends to unwind around March opex, whereas June follows a spring push with less stored energy, so June is usually less bad than March.
claims.indicator: quarterly options expiration (opex) cycle; month of year
claims.direction: weakness after Feb opex into March; milder June
claims.testable: yes - S&P returns around quarterly opex dates
